title: Open-ended curricula that create externally verified new competencies

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a learning system that repeatedly chooses new tasks for itself, learns to perform them, and accumulates competencies that were absent from its designers’ original task list. Its output would include both demonstrated skills and artifacts from which an independent learner could acquire those skills. External tests would establish that the growing inventory represents usable competence rather than increasingly elaborate task descriptions or self-assigned scores.

This entry adopts a stronger scope requirement than open-endedness defined through observer-relative novelty and learnability: progress must extend beyond improving a supplied evaluation target. That is a boundary proposed for this innovation, not a universal definition of open-endedness. Hughes and colleagues recognize narrow and finitely open-ended systems, including AlphaGo operating under fixed game rules, and discuss autonomous goal generation as one research direction within the broader field.

The intended learning loop connects task generation, practice, verification and reuse. New tasks must remain challenging enough to expand competence while remaining learnable; successful skills must become resources for subsequent learning. The reviewed position paper discusses adaptive task generation and describes Voyager as combining an LLM-driven curriculum with a library of verified, reusable skills. These provide technical precedents for parts of the proposed loop, without establishing its full cross-domain capability.

significance.text: If achieved, the direct advance would be sustained growth of an independently checked skill inventory after designers stop supplying additional objectives and datasets. The system would participate in deciding what to learn next, expanding the range of tasks it can perform over the demonstrated period. This would extend autonomous learning beyond better performance on an experimenter’s existing task list.

The significance does not depend on assuming that models trained on fixed corpora cannot produce novel results. Hughes and colleagues discuss how context, recombination and interaction complicate that restriction, while AlphaEvolve reports discoveries made with foundation models, search and automatic evaluation. The proposed additional capability concerns autonomous generation of learning targets and accumulation of externally verified competencies; novelty within a supplied problem can already be scientifically important.

As a conditional consequence, reusable competencies could support progressively richer curricula and reduce the need for people to enumerate every intermediate learning objective. Such a system might become useful in scientific investigation or control, but usefulness would depend on the quality, relevance and cost of its generated tasks. Growing a skill inventory would not by itself establish general intelligence, discovery of natural laws, economical learning, or reliable operation in the physical world.

The supplied research’s broader novelty-engine analogy is useful only at the level of repeatedly producing new, learnable outputs. It does not establish a historical equivalence or guarantee valuable discoveries. Likewise, observed growth would support a claim about the experiment’s duration and conditions, not unlimited future progress or retention over years.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability targeted here is an integrated process that autonomously proposes learning goals beyond the initial task specification, masters them, and continues building externally checkable competence. Generating candidate tasks alone is insufficient: the tasks must expose something new to a specified observer and remain learnable. Hughes and colleagues identify the adaptation of task difficulty to an agent’s changing capabilities as a promising approach, but this does not supply a demonstrated solution to the stronger capability defined here.

Engineering synthesis: task selection must avoid both trivial variations and goals that are currently impossible to learn. It must also distinguish substantive new competence from renamed versions of old tasks. This requires explicit novelty rules relative to the initial specification and a way to assess whether successive tasks demand additional capabilities. Otherwise, a longer task list could conceal little actual growth.

Engineering synthesis: autonomous goal generation creates a verification problem. A system that proposes a task and writes its only success test can reward its own mistakes or exploit weaknesses in that test. Independent evaluation must establish successful performance without requiring designers to specify all future destinations in advance. Separately, an independent learner must be able to acquire the skill from the system’s artifacts; successful execution by the originating system does not establish that form of learnability.

Engineering synthesis: skills must remain usable as new ones are added, and earlier competencies must support later learning rather than merely occupy an archive. Cross-domain growth also requires mechanisms that carry useful learning across different task formats and verification methods. Compute cost, verification cost and, for physical control, the consequences of unsuccessful exploration would constrain practical deployment even if a bounded demonstration succeeded.

current_state.text: In their position paper submitted on 6 June 2024, Hughes, Dennis, Parker-Holder, Behbahani, Mavalankar, Shi, Schaul and Rocktäschel describe open-ended, ever-improving AI as an elusive goal and develop an account based on observer-relative novelty and learnability. They also recognize existing narrow and finitely open-ended systems. Their discussion therefore supports a research direction and distinctions among forms of open-endedness, rather than a blanket claim that no open-ended systems exist.

Existing components discussed in that paper include fixed-rule self-play and generated curricula with reusable skills. AlphaGo illustrates why fixed rules do not automatically rule out open-endedness under the paper’s definition. Voyager illustrates curriculum construction and verified skill-library reuse. These examples help locate the proposed innovation: neither example, as characterized in the supplied review, establishes sustained, independently audited accumulation of new competencies across multiple domains under this entry’s stronger requirements.

The AlphaEvolve paper submitted on 16 June 2025 reports a nearby algorithm-discovery achievement: a rank-48 tensor-decomposition procedure for multiplying two 4×4 complex-valued matrices, using 48 complex scalar multiplications rather than the 49 in Strassen’s construction for this setting. The paper presents this as an improvement after 56 years. The comparison concerns the specified tensor-decomposition setting and scalar-multiplication count; it is not a claim of superiority over every possible multiplication procedure or of lower total runtime in every implementation.

AlphaEvolve’s user supplies the task and a mechanism for automatically evaluating generated solutions. Its reported discovery demonstrates that search within a supplied evaluation loop can produce an important new algorithm. It does not establish autonomous invention of evaluation targets or the broader curriculum capability proposed here. The supplied records are arXiv papers; the review does not establish their peer-review status or independent reproduction of the matrix construction.

The original research consulted AlphaEvolve’s abstract, while the supplied review additionally assessed relevant portions of its paper. The retained PDF extraction ends during page 36, but the review reports that the evaluation-method sections and the matrix result and comparison limits on page 10 are intact. No external construction notebook was supplied or inspected in that review. These access limits leave the reported result available as evidence within its stated scope, without establishing an independent reconstruction of it.

The supplied evidence does not establish whether this entry’s stronger capability remained undemonstrated as of 1 November 2026. No bounded freshness-search record was supplied. The dated achievements above can be described, but neither a present-day absence claim nor a claim that the proposed innovation has been achieved follows from this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: freeze the initial objective, seed dataset, initial task specification and permitted information sources, then run the system unattended for a pre-registered period. Record generated tasks, learning artifacts, evaluations, resource use and any human intervention. These are proposed experimental controls for attributing subsequent growth, not established standards for open-endedness.
completion_criteria.label: Unattended runs use frozen controls and record complete experimental histories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed independent audit: sample tasks from successive time windows under a pre-registered sampling rule. Count a competency only when auditors establish novelty relative to the initial task specification and verify the system’s performance using a test the system did not write. Audit rules should distinguish substantive additions from superficial task variants. Higher scores on an experimenter-supplied benchmark alone would not satisfy this proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Auditors verify substantive novelty and performance using independently written tests

completion_criteria.text: Proposed learnability and retention checks: an independent learner should acquire each sampled skill from the system’s artifacts, rather than merely observe a successful demonstration. Auditors should also retest earlier skills after later learning. This would distinguish transferable, retained competencies from isolated successes and would test whether the usable inventory actually grows.
completion_criteria.label: Sampled skills transfer through artifacts and survive later learning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility checks: demonstrate growth in retained competencies across at least two domains, such as formal problem solving and control of a physical or simulated plant. Repeat the protocol in independent runs and, where feasible, with an independent group. Report information access, computation, verification effort, failures and intervention requirements. The two-domain threshold is a proposed test of breadth; a simulated control result would establish that scope, without automatically establishing physical-world competence.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible retained competency growth spans at least two domains

completion_criteria.text: A successful finite experiment would establish sustained growth over its observed duration, task sample and operating conditions. It would not establish endless progress, literal universality, or years-long retention. Hughes and colleagues’ distinction between finite observation horizons and broader open-endedness supports keeping those conclusions separate.
completion_criteria.label: Conclusions remain bounded by observed duration, tasks and operating conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MLC-03, Cumulative learning without forgetting or loss of plasticity, overlaps through the need to retain earlier skills while learning new ones. MLC-07 concerns where new learning goals come from and whether they yield verified competencies; MLC-03 concerns maintaining cumulative learning capacity. MLC-05, Local credit assignment that matches backpropagation at scale, concerns the learning mechanism. MLC-07 does not require that mechanism to be local.

Roster-based synthesis: MLC-08, Discovery of new empirical laws, confirmed by experiment, could be a downstream application of generated curricula, but requires a distinct scientific outcome and experimental confirmation. A new mathematical algorithm or a growing skill library does not by itself constitute a new empirical law. The research’s broader novelty-engine framing can overlap both entries without merging their completion conditions.

Roster-based synthesis: MLC-02, Domain learning at a human experience budget, concerns learning efficiency; MLC-09, Skill learning from scarce, irreversible, real-world outcomes, concerns difficult feedback and exploration conditions; and MLC-11, Frontier competence at a biological-order power budget, concerns energy efficiency. An MLC-07 system could generate and learn new tasks while remaining expensive, data-hungry or limited to reversible simulations. Those constraints require separate demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis: MLC-04, World models that survive novel interventions, could support generated tasks involving control and prediction, but verified skill growth does not automatically establish robust world models. MLC-01, A predictive theory of what deep networks learn, concerns explaining or predicting learning behavior; MLC-07 is an operational capability that could be demonstrated without such a theory.

Roster-based synthesis: MLC-06, Algorithmic legibility sufficient to verify and edit a model, concerns understanding and changing internal computation. MLC-10, Non-vacuous behavioral certificates at frontier scale, concerns meaningful behavioral guarantees. Independent tests of newly learned skills provide evidence of sampled performance, without establishing internal legibility or certificates covering broader behavior. These distinctions use the supplied roster titles; detailed specifications for the other entries were not supplied.

change_log.change: Preserved MLC-07 and its title while defining autonomous task generation and externally verified skill accumulation as the central capability.
change_log.reason: The review supports the concept’s value despite corrections needed to its supporting claims.

change_log.change: Recast invention of new evaluation targets as this entry’s stronger scope requirement.
change_log.reason: Hughes and colleagues recognize fixed-rule and finitely open-ended systems, so that requirement cannot define all open-endedness.

change_log.change: Removed the categorical restriction of foundation-model deployment to its training distribution.
change_log.reason: The reviewed sources discuss contextual recombination and report novel discoveries using foundation models, search and evaluation.

change_log.change: Integrated adaptive task difficulty, verified skill reuse and the distinction between successful execution and independent learnability.
change_log.reason: These details explain the learning loop and prevent task success from being mistaken for transferable competence.

change_log.change: Specified AlphaEvolve’s rank-48 result, complex scalar-multiplication count, rank-49 comparison and tensor-decomposition scope.
change_log.reason: The numerical result is supported, but its historical comparison does not cover every multiplication procedure or runtime measure.

change_log.change: Preserved the supplied review’s AlphaEvolve extraction and access limitations.
change_log.reason: Relevant paper sections were assessed despite a truncated extraction; no external construction notebook or independent reconstruction was established.

change_log.change: Replaced the assertion that no later demonstration was found with an explicit freshness limitation.
change_log.reason: No search record establishes the state of the stronger capability through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration with temporal sampling, independent learning, retention checks, repeated runs and practical resource boundaries.
change_log.reason: These distinguish a growing usable skill inventory from selected successes while retaining the proposal’s experimental character.

change_log.change: Limited impact claims to demonstrated duration and breadth and explained relationships to the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: Finite evidence cannot establish indefinite growth, universality, natural-law discovery or the separate capabilities named by other entries.

unresolved_issues: Whether any later system demonstrates this entry’s stronger capability remains unresolved; the supplied record lacks a bounded freshness search through 1 November 2026.
Operational rules for substantive task novelty, the independent learner’s baseline and allowed resources, adequate retention, and meaningful growth remain to be specified.
Run duration, sampling coverage, resource budgets and reproducibility requirements remain proposed design choices rather than established thresholds.
The supplied review does not establish independent reproduction of AlphaEvolve’s rank-48 construction or assess an external construction notebook; its retained paper extraction is partial.
Only titles were supplied for the other roster entries, so detailed cross-entry boundaries and the broader historical novelty-engine comparison remain provisional.

brief.title: AI that chooses and learns new skills on its own
possible: Researchers could use an AI that keeps expanding what it can do after they stop giving it new learning goals. It would choose tasks beyond its original list, master them and leave materials that another learner could use to acquire the same skills.
Independent tests would confirm that its growing skill collection works. Earlier skills would remain usable and help it learn later ones.
why: People would need to spell out fewer intermediate learning goals. A system could help decide what to learn next, extending autonomous learning beyond improving performance on a list its designers supplied.
Reusable skills could support increasingly rich learning programmes. This could help scientific investigation or the control of machines by letting later learning build on earlier successes.

sources.who: Edward Hughes and colleagues at Google DeepMind
sources.showed: Their position paper defines open-ended learning through outputs that remain new and learnable to an observer. It discusses systems that generate learning tasks and reuse skills.
sources.cited_for: It provides a framework for judging continuing novelty and learnability, alongside examples of parts of the proposed learning loop.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate sustained, independently tested growth of new skills across different fields.

sources.who: Alexander Novikov and colleagues at Google DeepMind
sources.showed: AlphaEvolve generated new algorithms within tasks and automatic tests supplied by people. It found a matrix multiplication procedure using 48 scalar multiplications.
sources.quote:
Furthermore, AlphaEvolve discovered
novel, provably correct algorithms that surpass state-of-the-art solutions on a spectrum of problems
in mathematics and computer science, significantly expanding the scope of prior automated discovery
methods (Romera-Paredes et al., 2023).
sources.cited_for: It shows that AI can discover new algorithms while working towards a supplied goal.
sources.not_established: It does not show autonomous choice of learning goals, and independent reproduction of the matrix result remains unestablished.

shown: Voyager combines AI-generated learning tasks with a library of checked, reusable skills. Google DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve reports new algorithms, including a more efficient way to multiply matrices under a specific measure of arithmetic work.
These achievements demonstrate parts of the proposed capability. AlphaEvolve’s goals and tests come from people; Voyager does not establish independently audited growth across different fields.
missing: An integrated system must choose goals beyond its original task list, master them and keep accumulating independently tested skills.
Independent tests must distinguish substantive new abilities from renamed tasks and success on weak tests.
Another learner must acquire the skills from the system’s materials, while the original system retains earlier skills.
Repeated runs must demonstrate retained skill growth across different fields.

milestones.label: Unattended learning with fixed starting conditions and complete histories
milestones.explanation: An unattended run would keep its starting goals, data and allowed information sources fixed while logging tasks, learning, tests, resources and human help. This would make the source of later growth assessable.

milestones.label: Independent tests confirm new skills
milestones.explanation: Auditors would sample tasks over time under a preset rule and confirm novelty and performance using tests they write independently. This would distinguish added abilities from superficial task variations.

milestones.label: Skills can be taught and remain usable
milestones.explanation: An independent learner would acquire sampled skills from the system’s materials, and earlier skills would pass retests after later learning. This would establish a growing collection of transferable, retained abilities.

milestones.label: Repeated growth across at least two fields
milestones.explanation: Repeated independent runs would show retained skill growth across at least two fields, with costs, failures and human help reported. This would test breadth and reproducibility.

milestones.label: Claims stay within observed limits
milestones.explanation: Conclusions would describe growth only over the tested duration, tasks and conditions. This would keep a finite success from being mistaken for proof of endless progress or universal ability.

uncertain: What counts as a substantive new skill, and how much prior knowledge and help should an independent learner have?
How long must growth and retention last, and how much sampling and repetition would make the result convincing?
Would the generated skills be useful enough to justify the cost of learning and independently testing them?
